name: Northern Ireland
summary_text: Northern Ireland stands within the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 framework, in which the Supreme Court's ruling now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery. In August 2026 the UK equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. Trans visitors to Northern Ireland therefore use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.  Prison placement and searching follow the parent framework. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; the same argument had been aired in that court on 5 February 2026, where government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. On 17 April 2025 British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy to treat trans women as strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth, and on 25 June 2025 Police Scotland published interim guidance placing custody searches and stop-and-search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear on biological sex, while endeavouring to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request.  Northern Ireland's own education authorities have moved against trans-inclusive practice. On 8 September 2025 BBC News reported that guidance supporting transgender pupils was withdrawn from the Northern Ireland Education Authority's website after Education Minister Paul Givan requested its removal, arguing that it conflicted with departmental policy and with the law in Northern Ireland. The withdrawn guidance had recommended that trans pupils be allowed to use changing rooms matching their gender identity, and teachers' representatives warned that its removal ignores the practical realities faced in schools.  Protection machinery in Northern Ireland remains incomplete. On 14 December 2025 BBC News reported that other Northern Ireland Executive parties blocked Justice Minister Naomi Long's plan to add transgender people as a protected characteristic in the region's new hate-crime legislation. Long had sought executive approval in early November 2025 with a response deadline in mid-November, against a bill that had held executive agreement since December 2024, and she cited Police Service of Northern Ireland statistics of close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes.  Northern Ireland sits on equality legislation different from the Great Britain statute and is still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling, so the precise reach of the single-sex provisions in local equality law is not yet settled by any Northern Ireland court.  Gender recognition documents carry entry and administrative consequences across the United Kingdom. In December 2023 the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the ground that those jurisdictions allowed people to transition too easily; people from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change their gender in the UK. Within the United Kingdom a certificate will not be issued unless the applicant's spouse consents, and if the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated.  Access to gender-affirming care for minors is restricted under the parent framework. NHS England stopped prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people in March 2024, renewed that suspension indefinitely in December 2024 with reconsideration due in 2027, and by April 2025 had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year following the Cass Review of April 2024, which also led to the closure of the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024. Schools and sport carry parallel exclusions: the Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a gender recognition certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams, while transgender youth are otherwise covered by the Equality Act 2010.

name: Scotland
summary_text: Scotland stands under the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 regime, which now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The daily consequence for a trans visitor in Scotland is that facilities designated by biological sex are the ones to be used, with organisations instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.  Prison placement has been litigated to the same end. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The competing arguments were aired in the same court on 5 February 2026, when it was argued that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard and For Women Scotland pressed its challenge to the policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.  Searching and strip-searching policy follows the same principle. On 17 April 2025 British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, adopting an interim position that trans women are strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth; the prior policy had permitted trans women staff to intimately search women holding a gender recognition certificate, and Sex Matters welcomed the change. On 25 June 2025 Police Scotland published interim guidance under which searches in custody and stop-and-search involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, with efforts made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request where lived gender differs.  Gender recognition documents carry their own consequences. In December 2023 the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the ground that those jurisdictions allowed people to transition too easily; people from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change their gender in the UK. The Women and Equalities Minister, Kemi Badenoch, called the changes long overdue, while Shadow Equalities Minister Anneliese Dodds warned of diplomatic consequences because the list excluded Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Within the UK, a certificate will not be issued unless the applicant's spouse consents; where the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated, and transgender people seeking a certificate have historically been required to divorce or annul first.  Access to gender-affirming care is restricted for minors. NHS England said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people, a suspension renewed indefinitely in December 2024 and due to be reconsidered in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the NHS had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the Cass Review, with some families turning to black-market or overseas hormones instead. The Cass Review of April 2024 also led NHS England to close the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services. Bell v Tavistock (December 2020) had found that children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers; that judgment was overturned on appeal in September 2021.  Restrictions reach schools and sport. The Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a gender recognition certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams. Transgender youth are otherwise covered by the Equality Act 2010. On 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.  Scotland operates its own hate-crime machinery, and charges carrying a transgender-identity aggravation are rising. The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service reported in Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26, published 30 June 2026, that 7,115 hate-crime charges were brought in 2025-26, up 17 per cent on 2024-25 and the highest total since 2003-04. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, a rise of 21 per cent from 86 and the highest level recorded since the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021 took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category. A trans visitor therefore enters a jurisdiction where trans-motivated offences are actively charged under a dedicated statutory aggravator, at a level the prosecuting service describes as the highest since the provision began.

On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The competing arguments were aired in the same court on 5 February 2026, when it was argued that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard and For Women Scotland pressed its challenge to the policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.  Searching and strip-searching policy follows the same principle. On 17 April 2025 British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, adopting an interim position that trans women are strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth; the prior policy had permitted trans women staff to intimately search women holding a gender recognition certificate, and Sex Matters welcomed the change. On 25 June 2025 Police Scotland published interim guidance under which searches in custody and stop-and-search involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, with efforts made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request where lived gender differs.  Gender recognition documents carry their own consequences. In December 2023 the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the ground that those jurisdictions allowed people to transition too easily; people from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change their gender in the UK. The Women and Equalities Minister, Kemi Badenoch, called the changes long overdue, while Shadow Equalities Minister Anneliese Dodds warned of diplomatic consequences because the list excluded Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Within the UK, a certificate will not be issued unless the applicant's spouse consents; where the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated, and transgender people seeking a certificate have historically been required to divorce or annul first.  Access to gender-affirming care is restricted for minors. NHS England said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people, a suspension renewed indefinitely in December 2024 and due to be reconsidered in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the NHS had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the Cass Review, with some families turning to black-market or overseas hormones instead. The Cass Review of April 2024 also led NHS England to close the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services. Bell v Tavistock (December 2020) had found that children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers; that judgment was overturned on appeal in September 2021.  Restrictions reach schools and sport. The Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a gender recognition certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams. Transgender youth are otherwise covered by the Equality Act 2010. On 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.  Scotland operates its own hate-crime machinery, and charges carrying a transgender-identity aggravation are rising. The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service reported in Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26, published 30 June 2026, that 7,115 hate-crime charges were brought in 2025-26, up 17 per cent on 2024-25 and the highest total since 2003-04. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, a rise of 21 per cent from 86 and the highest level recorded since the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021 took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category. A trans visitor therefore enters a jurisdiction where trans-motivated offences are actively charged under a dedicated statutory aggravator, at a level the prosecuting service describes as the highest since the provision began.
